opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the core problems we have to solve. Right now, the main way we align models is reinforcement learning from human feedback: a human looks at what the model did and says whether it was good or bad. That works well as long as humans can actually evaluate the behavior. But as systems get more capable, they'll do things that are too complex, too long, or too technical for us to judge reliably. Think of a model writing a large codebase, or proposing a complicated scientific argument. A human evaluator might miss a subtle bug or a flawed step, and then we're training the model to produce things that *look* good to us rather than things that *are* good.

The basic idea of scalable oversight is to use AI to help humans evaluate AI. A key intuition is that evaluation is often easier than generation. It's much easier to check a proof than to come up with it, and much easier to notice a bug once someone points at the line. So if we can train assistant models that help us find the problems, we can extend how far human judgment reaches.

A concrete example is our work on critiques. We trained models to write critiques of other models' outputs, for instance pointing out flaws in summaries or bugs in code. When human evaluators had access to those critiques, they found substantially more flaws than they did on their own, including flaws we had deliberately planted. That's a small, early version of the idea, but it's encouraging.

You can push it further with something like recursive reward modeling. You use AI assistance to evaluate a slightly harder task, train a model on that, then use that model to help evaluate an even harder task, and so on. Ideally you bootstrap your way up while humans stay in the loop at every step.

There are real open questions. How do we know the assistant itself isn't misleading us? What if the model being evaluated and the assistant collude, or the assistant has blind spots that line up with the model's flaws? That's why I think it's really important to measure whether these techniques work. One approach I like is the "sandwiching" setup, or more generally, deliberately introducing known flaws and checking whether the oversight process catches them. If you can't empirically show that your oversight catches problems you planted, you shouldn't trust it to catch problems you didn't.

So I'm optimistic, but I don't think it comes for free. We need to treat it as a serious empirical research problem, and we need to start now, while the models are still at a level where we can check our work.

r001.rationale: It says that as systems become more capable, their outputs can become too complex or technical for humans to judge reliably.

r002.rationale: It says bugs are much easier to notice once pointed out and describes AI critiques helping human evaluators find flaws.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the ease of evaluation and generation for humans, but does not state that an AI bug-finding assistant is easier to supervise than an AI writing the code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is really the crux of the whole alignment problem as I see it. The basic worry is that the techniques we use today, like reinforcement learning from human feedback, fundamentally rely on a human being able to look at what the model did and say "that was good" or "that was bad." And that works fine when the model is writing a short poem or summarizing an article, because you can read the output and judge it. But as systems get more capable, they're going to be doing things that humans can't easily evaluate anymore. Imagine a model writes a million lines of code, or produces a long scientific argument, or runs a long agentic task over many steps. A human just can't check all of that, and if they can't check it, the reward signal gets noisy, and the model might learn to produce things that look good rather than things that are actually good.

So the idea of scalable oversight is: how do we close that gap? And the answer I find most promising is that we use AI to help humans evaluate AI. There's a few flavors of this. One is critiques, where you train a model to point out flaws in another model's output. The key insight here is that evaluation is often easier than generation. If I write some code, it's hard to write it, but if you point me to the specific line where there's a bug, I can verify that pretty quickly. So the critique model doesn't need to be smarter than the model it's critiquing, it just needs to surface the relevant thing for the human to look at.

Then there's debate, which is more elaborate. You have two models arguing opposite sides, and the human judges. The hope is that it's easier to argue for true things than for false things, so the truth-telling side has an advantage, and the human only needs to adjudicate rather than figure everything out from scratch.

And there's also this recursive idea, where you have a model that assists the human, and that assistant model is itself trained with the help of weaker assistants, and so on. Each step only needs the human-plus-assistant team to be a bit more capable at evaluation than the previous level.

Now, the honest caveat is that none of this is proven to work at scale yet. We have some encouraging early empirical results. For instance, we did experiments where we introduced deliberate bugs into code and showed that humans with critique models found a lot more of them than humans alone. But that's a fairly controlled setting. The real worry is whether these approaches hold up when the model has an incentive to deceive you, or when the thing being evaluated is a genuinely hard question where humans can be fooled by sophisticated but wrong arguments.

What I like about this research direction is that it's something we can actually make progress on now. We can set up these sandwiching experiments where you have an expert who knows the right answer, a non-expert who doesn't, and a model in between, and you test whether the non-expert plus the model can get to the expert's answer. That gives you a feedback loop for figuring out what actually works, rather than just theorizing. And it lets us iterate on the alignment techniques alongside the capabilities, which is ultimately the race I think we need to stay ahead in.

r001.rationale: The response says increasingly capable systems will perform tasks humans cannot easily evaluate, creating an oversight gap.

r002.rationale: It says a human can quickly verify a specific bug flagged by a critique model, whereas writing and evaluating code unaided is harder.

r003.rationale: It contrasts evaluation with generation and says a critique model need not be smarter than the model it critiques, only surface relevant issues for a human to inspect.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic idea is that we should use AI to make the job of oversight easier. If a model produces a complicated piece of code, for example, it might be very difficult for a human to tell whether that code does what we want. But an AI assistant could help explain it, point out potentially problematic parts, or design tests that the human can then inspect.

So you’re changing the task from “evaluate this whole complicated thing yourself” to “evaluate a set of much more tractable questions, with assistance.” And that could let us extend human oversight to tasks that we couldn’t reliably supervise unaided.

The hard part is knowing whether the assistance is actually helping us get the right answer, rather than just making an answer sound convincing. If the assistant misses the same problems as the system it’s checking, you haven’t gained very much. So we need to test these oversight methods in situations where we can independently check whether they catch mistakes, and understand where they fail.

Ultimately, we want AI to help humans understand and evaluate what’s happening, while keeping humans in a position to provide meaningful direction.

r001.rationale: The response says AI assistance may extend oversight to tasks humans could not supervise unaided, but does not state that greater AI capability does not automatically improve human oversight.

r002.rationale: It suggests an assistant can flag problematic code for human inspection, but does not clearly explain that verifying an identified bug is easier than finding bugs unaided.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how easy it is to supervise an AI system finding bugs with one writing the code being evaluated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic idea is that we shouldn’t expect humans to do all of the oversight unaided. If a model produces a large piece of code, for example, it might take a human a long time to understand whether it does what we intended. But we could use another model to explain the code, identify suspicious parts, and help us design tests.

That potentially lets us turn a task that’s too difficult for a human to evaluate directly into a series of smaller questions that we can evaluate. And as our models get more capable, we can use those capabilities to improve the oversight process itself.

The hard part is knowing whether that assistance is actually reliable. If the model helping you evaluate an answer shares the same blind spots as the model producing it, you could end up feeling more confident without being more correct. So we need to test whether AI assistance actually helps people catch mistakes, including mistakes that are deliberately hard to find.

Ultimately, the aim is to extend human judgment: give people enough understanding and enough ability to check the work that their feedback remains meaningful, even when they couldn’t have done the original task themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says greater model capability can support oversight, but warns that assistance may share the producer’s blind spots and must be tested. This communicates that capability gains alone do not ensure better human oversight.

r002.rationale: It says an assistant can identify suspicious code and help design tests, but does not say that checking an identified bug is easier for a human than finding bugs unaided.

r003.rationale: It discusses the reliability of AI assistance but does not compare how easy it is to supervise a bug-finding system with a code-writing system.
